title: The Python mental model
summary: Understand names, objects, mutability, and why Python behaves the way it does.
why: Many Python bugs are not syntax bugs. They come from misunderstanding references. Once you know that a variable is a name pointing at an object, assignments, lists, and function arguments become much easier to reason about.

sections.heading: Names point to objects
sections.body: Python variables do not contain boxes of values in the way a beginner often imagines. A name points to an object. Assignment makes another name point to the same object; it does not automatically copy it.
bullets: Immutable objects include integers, strings, and tuples.
Mutable objects include lists, dictionaries, and sets.
Use == to compare values and is only when identity truly matters.

sections.heading: The classic list alias
sections.body: If two names point to one list, changing the list through either name is visible through both names. This is useful when sharing state intentionally, but surprising when you expected a copy.
bullets: Use items.copy() for a shallow list copy.
Use copy.deepcopy() only when nested mutable objects also need copying.
Function arguments pass object references; the function can mutate a mutable object.

sections.heading: A reliable debugging habit
sections.body: When behavior surprises you, inspect the value and its type first. Then ask: did I create a new object, or did I reuse an existing object? This question solves a large class of beginner bugs.

code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
alias = numbers
copy = numbers.copy()

alias.append(4)
print(numbers)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(copy)    # [1, 2, 3]

name = "Ada"
other_name = name
print(name == other_name)  # True
mistakes: Using is to compare strings or numbers.
Assuming list assignment creates a copy.
Using a mutable list as a default function argument.
takeaways: A variable is a name bound to an object.
Mutation changes an existing object; reassignment changes what a name points to.
Prefer explicit copies when ownership should be separate.

title: Functions that are easy to trust
summary: Design small functions with clear inputs, outputs, type hints, and tests.
why: Functions are the smallest reusable unit in a Python application. Good function boundaries make algorithms testable, APIs understandable, and future changes safer.

sections.heading: One job, one contract
sections.body: A useful function has a focused responsibility. Its parameters describe the input, its return value describes the output, and its docstring explains the rule that is not obvious from the name.
bullets: Prefer return over print inside reusable logic.
Keep input validation close to the boundary.
Name functions with verbs: calculate_total, parse_user, find_missing.

sections.heading: Default arguments are evaluated once
sections.body: Default values are created when Python defines the function, not each time the function runs. A mutable default can therefore leak data between calls.
bullets: Use None as the default sentinel for lists and dictionaries.
Create the mutable value inside the function.
Keyword-only arguments make important options explicit.

sections.heading: Test behavior, not implementation
sections.body: A small group of meaningful assertions gives a function a safety net. Include the normal case, an edge case, and an invalid or empty case when the contract allows them.

mistakes: Returning inconsistent types from different branches.
Hiding important side effects inside a function named like a calculation.
Skipping tests for empty input and boundary values.
takeaways: A function contract is its input, output, and failure behavior.
Type hints communicate intent; they do not replace validation.
Small pure functions are easier to test and reuse.

title: The standard library toolbox
summary: Choose Counter, defaultdict, deque, heapq, and set operations with confidence.
why: Strong Python problem solving is often about recognizing the right data structure quickly. The standard library gives you well-tested building blocks so you can focus on the idea instead of reimplementing them.

sections.heading: Count with Counter
sections.body: Counter is a dictionary specialized for frequencies. It makes anagram checks, top-frequency tasks, and histogram logic direct and readable.
bullets: Counter(text) counts each character.
most_common(k) returns the most frequent items.
A missing key behaves like a zero count.

sections.heading: Use deque for both ends
sections.body: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element and is O(n). deque.popleft() is O(1), which makes it the natural queue for BFS and sliding-window tasks.
bullets: append and pop from the right.
appendleft and popleft from the left.
Use maxlen for a bounded rolling buffer.

sections.heading: Sets express membership
sections.body: A set answers membership questions in average O(1) time. It is a strong fit for visited nodes, duplicate detection, and unique values.
bullets: Sets require hashable elements.
Use sorted(set(values)) when you need unique ordered output.
Do not use a list for repeated membership checks on large input.

sections.heading: Heaps keep the next best item
sections.body: heapq maintains a min-heap. It is useful when you repeatedly need the smallest item, or when you want a top-k algorithm without sorting everything.

code:
from collections import Counter, deque

text = "banana"
counts = Counter(text)
print(counts.most_common(2))

queue = deque(["learn", "practice"])
queue.append("review")
print(queue.popleft())

seen = set()
for value in [3, 3, 1, 2]:
    seen.add(value)
print(sorted(seen))
mistakes: Using a list as a queue and accidentally creating O(n) operations.
Sorting the full input when only the top few values are needed.
Putting lists or dictionaries directly inside a set.
takeaways: Pick a data structure based on the operation you repeat.
Counter is a readable frequency map.
deque is the default queue; set is the default membership structure.

title: Errors are part of the design
summary: Handle expected failures clearly with exceptions, context managers, and useful logs.
why: Production code meets missing files, bad input, timeouts, and network failures. Handling those cases intentionally makes software easier to operate and easier for users to recover from.

sections.heading: Catch only what you can handle
sections.body: A broad except Exception can hide programming bugs. Catch the specific failure you expect, add context, and either recover or re-raise when the caller needs to decide.
bullets: ValueError means the value has the wrong shape or meaning.
FileNotFoundError is more useful than a generic file error.
Never silently turn an error into a fake success.

sections.heading: Context managers close resources
sections.body: The with statement guarantees cleanup when a block ends, even when an exception is raised. Use it for files, database connections, and locks.
bullets: with open(...) as file closes the file automatically.
Keep the smallest useful block inside the context manager.
Use encoding="utf-8" for text files.

sections.heading: Logs explain the path to failure
sections.body: A user-facing message should be short and safe. A log should include enough context for a developer to diagnose the problem, without exposing passwords or private data.

mistakes: Catching every exception and continuing as if nothing happened.
Logging secrets, tokens, or full user input.
Opening files without a context manager.
takeaways: Expected failures belong in the function contract.
Catch narrowly and preserve the original cause with from.
Context managers make cleanup automatic.

title: Big-O: how fast does your code grow?
summary: Learn to count growth, not seconds, and to pick an algorithm from the input size.
why: Interview questions are never only about the right answer. They ask for the right answer that still works when the input is 100,000 items. Big-O is the language you use to compare solutions before you write them.

sections.heading: Count steps, not seconds
sections.body: Seconds change from laptop to laptop, but the number of steps as the input n grows does not. Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing part and drops constants, so 3n + 10 becomes O(n).
bullets: Single loop over n items: O(n).
Loop inside a loop over the same data: O(n^2).
Halving the problem each step (binary search): O(log n).

sections.heading: The classes you must know
sections.body: From fast to slow: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!). A dictionary lookup is O(1) on average, sorting is O(n log n), and checking every pair is O(n^2).
bullets: n = 1,000,000 with O(n^2) is about 10^12 steps, which is far too slow.
n log n for 10^6 is about 2 * 10^7 steps, which is fine.
Recursion that branches twice per call is often O(2^n).

sections.heading: Read the constraints
sections.body: The input limit tells you the target complexity. If n is up to 10^5, aim for O(n log n) or better. If n is up to 20, even O(2^n) can pass. This one habit saves hours of coding the wrong idea.
bullets: n <= 12: factorial is possible.
n <= 5000: O(n^2) is possible.
n <= 10^6: O(n log n) or O(n).

sections.heading: Space complexity
sections.body: Space counts the extra memory you use, not the input itself. Using a set to remember seen items is O(n) extra space. Often you trade memory for speed, and you should say so out loud in an interview.

sections.heading: Worked example: duplicates
sections.body: The slow way compares every pair, O(n^2) time with O(1) space. The fast way remembers what it has seen in a set, O(n) time with O(n) space. Same answer, very different growth.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these after reading:
bullets: Contains Duplicate (Easy)
Valid Anagram (Easy)
Two Sum (Easy)

mistakes: Counting constants instead of growth, such as calling 2n and n different classes.
Forgetting that slicing, sorting and `in list` are not free.
Ignoring space complexity when using sets and dictionaries.
takeaways: Big-O describes growth as the input becomes large.
Use the input limit to choose the target complexity first.
Trading space for time is normal; always state the trade.

title: Recursion and the call stack
summary: Think recursively: base case, smaller problem, and how memoization removes repeated work.
why: Trees, graphs, backtracking and dynamic programming all start with recursion. If you can trace a recursive call on paper, those topics become much easier.

sections.heading: The two rules
sections.body: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops, and a recursive case that moves toward the base case. Without the first it never ends; without the second it never makes progress.
bullets: Write the base case first.
Trust that the smaller call returns the right answer.
Combine the smaller answer into your answer.

sections.heading: The call stack
sections.body: Each call waits on the stack until the call it made returns. Python limits depth (about 1000 by default), so very deep recursion raises RecursionError. In that case convert the code to a loop or use an explicit stack.
bullets: Depth of the stack equals extra space, O(depth).
sys.setrecursionlimit exists but is not a fix for bad design.

sections.heading: Repeated work and memoization
sections.body: Naive Fibonacci recomputes the same values again and again, so it takes O(2^n) time. Storing results (memoization) makes each value computed once and the time O(n). This is the first step toward dynamic programming.
bullets: functools.lru_cache adds memoization with one line.
Arguments must be hashable to be cached.

sections.heading: Worked example: Fibonacci
sections.body: fib(15) with naive recursion makes 1973 calls. With a cache it makes only 16 distinct computations. Run the code and compare the call counter.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Try these:
bullets: Fibonacci Number (Easy)
Power of Two (Easy)
Climbing Stairs (Easy)

mistakes: Forgetting the base case, which causes RecursionError.
Not moving toward the base case (for example calling f(n) again).
Recomputing the same subproblem without a cache.
takeaways: Base case plus smaller problem is the whole pattern.
The call stack costs O(depth) memory.
Memoization turns exponential recursion into linear work.

title: Arrays: prefix sums and Kadane's algorithm
summary: Answer range-sum queries in O(1) and find the best subarray in one pass.
why: Arrays are the most common interview topic. Two small ideas, prefix sums and Kadane, solve a surprising number of problems with one pass.

sections.heading: Prefix sums
sections.body: Store running totals once, then any range sum is a subtraction: sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. Building costs O(n) once, and each query is O(1) afterward.
bullets: Use a leading 0 so l = 0 needs no special case.
Works for counts, 2D grids, and difference arrays too.

sections.heading: Kadane's algorithm
sections.body: To find the maximum subarray sum, walk once and decide at every item: extend the previous subarray or start fresh here. If the running sum becomes worse than the item itself, restart.
bullets: cur = max(x, cur + x)
best = max(best, cur)
Initialize with the first element so all-negative arrays work.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: For [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4], the best subarray is [4, -1, 2, 1] with sum 6. For [2, 4, 6, 8] the range sum from index 1 to 2 is 4 + 6 = 10.

sections.heading: In-place and edge cases
sections.body: Check empty arrays, one item, all negatives, and duplicates. Prefer in-place updates when the problem allows, but never mutate input silently if the caller still needs it.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these in order:
bullets: Maximum Subarray (Medium)
Range Sum Query - Immutable (Easy)
Product of Array Except Self (Medium)
Subarray Sum Equals K (Medium)

mistakes: Off-by-one in prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
Starting Kadane with 0, which breaks all-negative arrays.
Rebuilding the prefix array for every query.
takeaways: Prefix sums trade O(n) setup for O(1) queries.
Kadane decides extend-or-restart at each element.
Always test empty, single and all-negative inputs.

title: Strings: palindromes, anagrams and grouping
summary: Handle string problems with two pointers, frequency counts and canonical keys.
why: String questions are the easiest way for companies to test careful thinking. Most of them reduce to counting characters, two pointers, or building a clean key.

sections.heading: Strings are immutable
sections.body: In Python you cannot change a string in place. Repeated s += c can be slow, so collect pieces in a list and use ''.join(parts) at the end.
bullets: s[::-1] reverses a string.
str methods like isalnum() and lower() clean input.

sections.heading: Palindrome with two pointers
sections.body: Clean the text, then compare from both ends toward the middle. This is O(n) time and avoids reversing a copy when you want to save memory.
bullets: Ignore case and non-letters when the problem says so.
Stop when the pointers meet.

sections.heading: Anagrams with counts or sorted keys
sections.body: Two words are anagrams when they have the same character counts. For grouping, use the sorted letters as a dictionary key so all anagrams land in the same bucket.
bullets: Counter(a) == Counter(b) is O(n).
tuple(sorted(word)) is a hashable key.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: ['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat'] groups into [['eat','tea','ate'], ['tan','nat'], ['bat']] because their sorted letters match.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Solve these:
bullets: Valid Palindrome (Easy)
Valid Anagram (Easy)
Group Anagrams (Medium)
Longest Palindromic Substring (Medium)

mistakes: Comparing without cleaning case and punctuation.
Using a list (unhashable) as a dictionary key.
Concatenating strings in a loop for huge input.
takeaways: Strings are immutable; build with join.
Counts and sorted keys solve most anagram problems.
Two pointers solve palindrome checks in O(n).

title: Hashing: the Two Sum family
summary: Use dictionaries and sets to turn O(n^2) searching into O(n).
why: Hash maps are the single most useful tool in interviews. Whenever you think 'have I seen this before?' or 'what do I need to complete this pair?', a dictionary is probably the answer.

sections.heading: Why hashing is fast
sections.body: A dictionary finds a key in O(1) on average by turning the key into a number (hash) that points to a slot. That is why `x in set` is fast and `x in list` is slow on big data.
bullets: Keys must be hashable (int, str, tuple, not list).
Worst case is O(n) with many collisions, but this is rare.

sections.heading: Two Sum
sections.body: For each number, ask which value you still need: target - x. If it is already in the map, you are done; otherwise store x with its index.
bullets: One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.

sections.heading: Prefix sum plus hashmap
sections.body: To count subarrays with sum k, keep a running prefix sum and a map of how many times each prefix appeared. At each step add seen[prefix - k]. This beats the O(n^2) approach and handles negative numbers.
bullets: Start with seen = {0: 1} for subarrays beginning at index 0.

sections.heading: Longest consecutive sequence
sections.body: Put all numbers in a set. Only start counting from numbers that have no predecessor (x - 1 not in set), then extend upward. Each number is visited a constant number of times, so it is O(n).

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Solve these:
bullets: Two Sum (Easy)
Subarray Sum Equals K (Medium)
Longest Consecutive Sequence (Medium)
Top K Frequent Elements (Medium)

code:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                       # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []


def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = prefix = 0
    seen = {0: 1}                   # empty prefix
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count


def longest_consecutive(nums):
    values, best = set(nums), 0
    for x in values:
        if x - 1 not in values:     # x starts a run
            y = x
            while y + 1 in values:
                y += 1
            best = max(best, y - x + 1)
    return best


assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1]
assert two_sum([1, 2], 10) == []
assert subarray_sum([1, 1, 1], 2) == 2
assert subarray_sum([1, 2, 3], 3) == 2
assert subarray_sum([1, -1, 0], 0) == 3
assert longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]) == 4
print(longest_consecutive([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1]))   # 9
mistakes: Using the same element twice in Two Sum.
Forgetting seen = {0: 1} in the prefix-sum pattern.
Using sorting where a set gives O(n).
takeaways: Ask 'what do I need to complete the answer?' and look it up in a dict.
Prefix sum plus hashmap counts subarrays in O(n).
Sets give O(1) membership checks.

title: Two pointers on sorted data
summary: Move two indexes toward each other, or together, to remove a nested loop.
why: Two pointers is a simple trick that turns many O(n^2) searches into O(n) once the data is sorted or has a clear direction.

sections.heading: When it works
sections.body: Use two pointers when the array is sorted (or can be sorted) and you search for a pair or triple, or when you need to compress or partition an array in place.
bullets: Opposite ends moving inward: pair sums, container with most water.
Same direction (slow and fast): remove duplicates, move zeroes.

sections.heading: Pair sum on a sorted array
sections.body: If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right to increase it; if too big, move the right pointer left. Each pointer moves at most n times, so the total is O(n).
bullets: No extra memory needed.

sections.heading: 3Sum
sections.body: Sort the array, fix one number, and run two pointers on the rest. Skip duplicate values to avoid repeated triples. Total time is O(n^2), which is optimal for this problem.
bullets: Skip equal neighbors after finding a triple.

sections.heading: Container with most water
sections.body: Area is width times the shorter wall. Start with the widest container and always move the pointer at the shorter wall, because moving the taller one can never improve the area.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted (Medium)
3Sum (Medium)
Container With Most Water (Medium)
Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (Easy)

mistakes: Using two pointers on unsorted data without sorting first.
Not skipping duplicates in 3Sum.
Moving the wrong pointer in the container problem.
takeaways: Sorted order lets you decide which pointer to move.
Each pointer moves at most n steps, so the pass is O(n).
Sort first, then two pointers, gives O(n^2) for 3Sum.

title: Sliding window: fixed and variable
summary: Reuse work between neighboring subarrays instead of recalculating from scratch.
why: Any problem about a continuous part of an array or string (longest, shortest, maximum sum) is a sliding window candidate. It turns O(n*k) or O(n^2) into O(n).

sections.heading: Fixed-size window
sections.body: When the window size k is given, add the new element on the right and remove the old one on the left. The sum updates in O(1) instead of recomputing k numbers.
bullets: Maximum sum of k consecutive elements.
Average of every window.

sections.heading: Variable-size window
sections.body: Grow the right end to include more, and shrink the left end while the window is invalid (or while it is still valid, for a shortest-window question). Each element enters and leaves once, so it is O(n).
bullets: Longest substring without repeating characters: shrink while a duplicate exists.
Shortest subarray with sum >= target: shrink while the sum is still large enough.

sections.heading: The template
sections.body: Keep two pointers (left, right), a state (sum or counts), and an answer. For each right, update the state; while the window breaks the rule, update the state and move left; then update the answer.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: In 'abcabcbb' the window grows to 'abc' (3), sees another 'a', shrinks past the first 'a', and keeps going. The best length is 3. In [2,3,1,2,4,3] with target 7 the shortest subarray is [4,3] of length 2.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Maximum Average Subarray I (Easy)
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (Medium)
Minimum Size Subarray Sum (Medium)
Longest Repeating Character Replacement (Medium)

code:
def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]     # add new, remove old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best


def longest_unique(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1             # jump past the duplicate
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best


def min_len_subarray(target, nums):
    left = total = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:              # shrink while still valid
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best


assert max_sum_k([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3) == 9
assert longest_unique("abcabcbb") == 3 and longest_unique("") == 0
assert longest_unique("pwwkew") == 3
assert min_len_subarray(7, [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]) == 2
assert min_len_subarray(100, [1, 2, 3]) == 0
print(longest_unique("bbbbb"))   # 1
mistakes: Recomputing the whole window sum each step.
Moving left only once when you must shrink repeatedly (use while).
Forgetting to return 0 or -1 when no valid window exists.
takeaways: A window is a contiguous range with a maintained state.
Each element enters once and leaves once: O(n).
Fixed window: slide. Variable window: grow then shrink.

title: Binary search and binary search on the answer
summary: Cut the search space in half each step, on sorted data or on any yes/no answer range.
why: Binary search is one of the most tested topics. It also hides inside many 'find the minimum value that works' problems, which are solved by searching the answer itself.

sections.heading: Classic binary search
sections.body: On a sorted array, compare the middle item with the target and discard half. O(log n) time and O(1) space. Searching 1,000,000 items takes about 20 steps.
bullets: Pick one loop template (lo <= hi) and stay consistent.
Always move with mid + 1 or mid - 1 to avoid infinite loops.

sections.heading: Lower bound
sections.body: Lower bound finds the first index where nums[i] >= target. It is the base for first occurrence, insert position and counting duplicates. Python's bisect_left does the same.
bullets: Use lo < hi with hi = len(nums).
Keep mid in the range when it might be the answer (hi = mid).

sections.heading: Rotated sorted array
sections.body: In a rotated array one half around mid is always sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half and move to that half, else move to the other.
bullets: Compare nums[lo] <= nums[mid] to know which half is sorted.

sections.heading: Binary search on the answer
sections.body: If a value works then every bigger value also works (or the reverse), the yes/no pattern is monotonic. Search the answer range directly and test each guess with a simple function. Example: smallest eating speed that finishes all piles in h hours.
bullets: Write a helper can_do(x) first.
Set the bounds to the smallest and largest possible answers.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Binary Search (Easy)
Search Insert Position (Easy)
Search in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium)
Koko Eating Bananas (Medium)
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium)

mistakes: Mixing the lo <= hi and lo < hi templates.
Forgetting mid +/- 1, causing an infinite loop.
Using binary search on unsorted or non-monotonic data.
takeaways: Binary search needs sorted or monotonic data.
bisect_left is the lower bound; know both versions.
Search the answer when the question says 'minimum value such that'.

title: Sorting: merge sort, quick sort and intervals
summary: Understand how sorting works, why n log n is the target, and how sorting unlocks interval problems.
why: You will almost always call sorted() in real code, but interviews ask how sorting works and use sorting as the first step in many greedy and interval problems.

sections.heading: The sorting map
sections.body: Simple sorts (bubble, selection, insertion) are O(n^2) and only good for tiny or nearly sorted data. Merge sort and heap sort are O(n log n) always; quick sort is O(n log n) on average and O(n^2) in the worst case.
bullets: Python's sorted() uses Timsort: stable, O(n log n), fast on partly sorted data.
A stable sort keeps equal items in their original order.

sections.heading: Merge sort
sections.body: Split the array in half, sort each half, then merge two sorted halves with two pointers. Time is O(n log n) and it needs O(n) extra space. It is the clearest example of divide and conquer.

sections.heading: Quick sort
sections.body: Choose a pivot, put smaller items on the left and larger on the right, then sort both sides. A random pivot avoids the worst case. Quickselect uses the same idea to find the kth smallest in O(n) average time.

sections.heading: Sorting for intervals
sections.body: Sort intervals by start time, then merge while the next start is at most the current end. This turns a messy overlap problem into one clean pass after an O(n log n) sort.
bullets: Sort by end time for 'maximum non-overlapping' problems.
Use key=lambda x: x[0] to sort by a field.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Sort an Array (Medium)
Merge Intervals (Medium)
Kth Largest Element in an Array (Medium)
Sort Colors (Medium)

mistakes: Writing your own sort when sorted() is allowed.
Choosing the first element as pivot on already-sorted input.
Forgetting to sort intervals before merging.
takeaways: n log n is the standard sorting cost.
Merge sort is stable and predictable; quick sort is fast on average.
Sorting first often makes interval and greedy problems simple.

title: Linked lists: reverse, middle and cycle
summary: Master pointer manipulation with the three classic linked list patterns.
why: Linked lists test whether you can handle references carefully. The same three tricks (reverse, slow and fast pointers, dummy node) appear in dozens of interview questions.

sections.heading: What a linked list is
sections.body: A list of nodes where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. Inserting at the front is O(1), but reaching the kth item is O(k) because there is no indexing.
bullets: Python lists are arrays, not linked lists.
Always check for an empty list (head is None).

sections.heading: Reverse a list
sections.body: Walk through the list and flip each next pointer to point backward. Keep three names: prev, cur and nxt. Save cur.next before you overwrite it, or you lose the rest of the list.
bullets: O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.heading: Slow and fast pointers
sections.body: Move slow by one and fast by two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. If the list has a cycle, fast will eventually meet slow (Floyd's cycle detection).
bullets: Loop while fast and fast.next to avoid errors on None.

sections.heading: Dummy node for merging
sections.body: When you build a new list, start with a dummy head so the first node is not a special case. Return dummy.next at the end. Merge two sorted lists by always attaching the smaller head.
bullets: Worked example: merging [1,3,5] and [2,4,6] gives [1,2,3,4,5,6].

title: Stacks and the monotonic stack
summary: Use last-in-first-out thinking for brackets, min tracking and next-greater problems.
why: Stacks show up wherever the most recent unfinished item matters: brackets, undo, expression parsing and 'next greater element' questions.

sections.heading: Stack basics
sections.body: In Python a list works as a stack: append to push and pop to remove the top, both O(1). Use a stack when you must resolve the most recent open item first.
bullets: Do not use list.pop(0) for queues; use deque.
Check the stack is not empty before reading the top.

sections.heading: Valid parentheses
sections.body: Push opening brackets. On a closing bracket the top must be the matching opener. At the end the stack must be empty. The mapping dictionary keeps the code short.
bullets: Odd-length strings can fail fast.

sections.heading: Min stack
sections.body: To get the minimum in O(1), store with each pushed value the minimum so far. The stack always knows the current minimum without scanning.
bullets: Store (value, min_so_far) pairs.

sections.heading: Monotonic stack
sections.body: Keep a stack of indexes whose values are in decreasing order. When a new value is greater than the top, the top has found its 'next greater' answer. Every index is pushed and popped once, so the whole thing is O(n).
bullets: Daily temperatures: days until a warmer day.
Next greater element and largest rectangle in a histogram use the same pattern.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Valid Parentheses (Easy)
Min Stack (Medium)
Daily Temperatures (Medium)
Next Greater Element I (Easy)
Largest Rectangle in Histogram (Hard)

mistakes: Popping from an empty stack.
Not checking that the stack is empty at the end of bracket matching.
Storing values instead of indexes when the answer needs distances.
takeaways: Stack = most recent unfinished item first.
Store the running minimum alongside each value for O(1) min.
A monotonic stack solves next-greater problems in O(n).

title: Backtracking: subsets, permutations and combinations
summary: Explore all choices with the choose, explore, undo template.
why: When a problem says 'generate all' or 'find every way', backtracking is the tool. It is recursion with an undo step, and it is the foundation for N-Queens, Sudoku and word search.

sections.heading: The template
sections.body: Build the answer one choice at a time. Choose an option, recurse to explore the rest, then undo the choice so the next option starts clean. Record a result when the current path is complete.
bullets: path is the current partial answer.
path.pop() is the undo step.

sections.heading: Subsets
sections.body: For every element you either take it or skip it, so there are 2^n subsets. Recursing with a start index avoids duplicates and ordering problems.
bullets: [1,2,3] has 8 subsets.

sections.heading: Permutations
sections.body: At each position try every unused element. Track used values with a set or boolean list. There are n! permutations, so only small inputs are possible.
bullets: [1,2,3] has 6 permutations.

sections.heading: Pruning and combination sum
sections.body: Pruning means stopping early when a path cannot work. In combination sum, sort the candidates and stop as soon as the remaining target becomes negative. Pruning can turn an impossible search into a fast one.
bullets: Complexity is exponential, so reason about the size of the search tree.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Subsets (Medium)
Permutations (Medium)
Combination Sum (Medium)
Word Search (Medium)
N-Queens (Hard)

code:
def subsets(nums):
    result = []

    def dfs(start, path):
        result.append(path[:])              # copy the current path
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])            # choose
            dfs(i + 1, path)                # explore
            path.pop()                      # undo

    dfs(0, [])
    return result


def permutations(nums):
    result, used = [], [False] * len(nums)

    def dfs(path):
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(x)
            dfs(path)
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    dfs([])
    return result


def combination_sum(candidates, target):
    candidates, result = sorted(candidates), []

    def dfs(start, remain, path):
        if remain == 0:
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
            if candidates[i] > remain:      # prune
                break
            path.append(candidates[i])
            dfs(i, remain - candidates[i], path)   # i, not i+1: reuse allowed
            path.pop()

    dfs(0, target, [])
    return result


assert len(subsets([1, 2, 3])) == 8 and [] in subsets([1, 2, 3])
assert len(permutations([1, 2, 3])) == 6
assert combination_sum([2, 3, 6, 7], 7) == [[2, 2, 3], [7]]
assert combination_sum([2], 1) == []
print(subsets([1, 2]))   # [[], [1], [1, 2], [2]]
mistakes: Appending path itself instead of a copy (path[:]).
Forgetting the undo step.
Not pruning impossible branches.
takeaways: Choose, explore, undo is the whole template.
Subsets are 2^n and permutations are n!, so size matters.
Pruning is what makes backtracking practical.

title: Binary trees: DFS, BFS, height and diameter
summary: Traverse trees recursively and level by level, and compute height and diameter.
why: Trees are the most common data structure after arrays. Nearly every tree problem is a traversal with one extra small idea.

sections.heading: Tree vocabulary
sections.body: A binary tree node has a value and up to two children. The root is the top node, a leaf has no children, and height is the number of nodes (or edges) on the longest root-to-leaf path. Say which convention you use.
bullets: Balanced tree height is about log n.
A skewed tree has height n.

sections.heading: DFS traversals
sections.body: Preorder visits root, left, right. Inorder visits left, root, right (sorted order for a BST). Postorder visits left, right, root. All three are just different positions for the 'visit' line in the same recursion.
bullets: Recursive depth equals tree height.

sections.heading: BFS by levels
sections.body: Use a queue. For each level, process exactly the number of nodes currently in the queue, then add their children. This gives level order, right-side view and minimum depth.
bullets: Use collections.deque.

sections.heading: Height and diameter
sections.body: Height of a node is 1 + max(height of children). The diameter (longest path between any two nodes) at a node is left height + right height. Update a global best while computing heights, which gives O(n) total.
bullets: Worked example: tree [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] has height 3 and diameter 3 edges.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (Easy)
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (Medium)
Diameter of Binary Tree (Easy)
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (Medium)
Invert Binary Tree (Easy)

mistakes: Forgetting the base case for None.
Mixing up height in nodes versus edges.
Not processing the queue level by level when levels matter.
takeaways: All DFS orders differ only in when you visit the root.
BFS with a queue gives level order.
Diameter equals left height plus right height at the best node.

title: Binary search trees
summary: Use the BST ordering rule for search, insert, validation and kth smallest.
why: A BST gives sorted data with fast search. Interviews love it because one rule (left < node < right) solves many questions, and because a common validation mistake catches many candidates.

sections.heading: The BST rule
sections.body: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. Search, insert and delete take O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed.
bullets: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.

sections.heading: Search and insert
sections.body: Compare with the node and go left or right until you find the value or reach None. Insert places the new node at that empty spot.
bullets: Iterative versions use O(1) space.

sections.heading: Validate a BST
sections.body: Checking only the immediate children is wrong. Pass down a valid (low, high) range: every node must lie strictly inside the range inherited from its ancestors.
bullets: Use float('-inf') and float('inf') for the first bounds.

sections.heading: Kth smallest
sections.body: Because inorder is sorted, run an inorder traversal and stop at the kth visited node. Using a generator keeps it lazy and avoids building the whole list.
bullets: Worked example: inserting 5,3,7,2,4,6,8 and asking for k = 3 returns 4.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Validate Binary Search Tree (Medium)
Kth Smallest Element in a BST (Medium)
Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST (Medium)
Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree (Easy)

mistakes: Validating only parent and child instead of the full range.
Assuming a BST is balanced.
Mishandling duplicates without a clear rule.
takeaways: Left < node < right for the whole subtree, not just children.
Inorder of a BST is sorted.
Operations cost O(height).

title: Heaps and priority queues
summary: Use heapq for top-k, kth largest, merging sorted lists and running median.
why: When a question says 'the k largest', 'the next smallest' or 'the median of a stream', a heap is almost always the intended structure.

sections.heading: What a heap gives you
sections.body: A heap keeps the smallest item at the top. Push and pop cost O(log n), peeking costs O(1), and building a heap from a list costs O(n). Python's heapq is a min-heap on a plain list.
bullets: For a max-heap push negative values.
Tuples compare by the first item, which is how you attach priorities.

sections.heading: Top-k and kth largest
sections.body: Keep a min-heap of size k. For each new number push it and, if the size exceeds k, pop the smallest. The heap root is then the kth largest. This is O(n log k), better than sorting everything when k is small.

sections.heading: Merge k sorted lists
sections.body: Push the first item of each list with its list index. Pop the smallest, add it to the output, and push the next item from the same list. Total time is O(N log k).
bullets: heapq.merge does this for you.

sections.heading: Running median with two heaps
sections.body: Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, with sizes differing by at most one. The median is the top of the bigger heap, or the average of both tops.
bullets: Rebalance after each insert.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Kth Largest Element in an Array (Medium)
Top K Frequent Elements (Medium)
Merge k Sorted Lists (Hard)
Find Median from Data Stream (Hard)
Task Scheduler (Medium)

mistakes: Expecting heapq to be a max-heap.
Sorting everything when only the top k are needed.
Forgetting to rebalance the two heaps.
takeaways: heapq is a min-heap; negate for max.
A size-k heap gives top-k in O(n log k).
Two heaps maintain a running median.

title: Graphs: BFS, DFS and grid problems
summary: Represent graphs, find shortest paths in unweighted graphs, count components and islands.
why: Graphs model maps, networks, dependencies and grids. BFS and DFS are the two traversals behind most graph questions.

sections.heading: Representing a graph
sections.body: An adjacency list (dictionary of node to neighbors) uses O(V + E) space and is best for most problems. An adjacency matrix uses O(V^2). Decide if edges are directed or undirected and add both directions for undirected graphs.
bullets: Grids are graphs where neighbors are up, down, left and right.

sections.heading: BFS
sections.body: BFS explores level by level with a queue, so the first time it reaches a node is along the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Mark nodes visited when you push them, not when you pop them.
bullets: O(V + E) time.
Use it for shortest steps, minimum moves and spreading problems.

sections.heading: DFS
sections.body: DFS goes as deep as it can, then backtracks, using recursion or a stack. It is natural for connected components, cycle detection, path existence and flood fill.
bullets: Always keep a visited set to avoid infinite loops.

sections.heading: Grid problems
sections.body: Number of islands: loop over every cell, and when you find land, flood-fill the whole island and count one. The directions list [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)] keeps neighbor code short.
bullets: Check bounds before indexing.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Number of Islands (Medium)
Flood Fill (Easy)
Rotting Oranges (Medium)
Clone Graph (Medium)
Find if Path Exists in Graph (Easy)

mistakes: Marking visited on pop instead of push in BFS (duplicates in the queue).
Not adding both directions for an undirected edge.
Indexing the grid before checking bounds.
takeaways: BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS is the natural tool for components and flood fill.
Always keep a visited set.

title: Weighted shortest path and topological sort
summary: Use a heap for Dijkstra and Kahn's algorithm for ordering tasks with dependencies.
why: Weighted paths and dependency ordering are the two graph ideas that appear most often after BFS and DFS: delivery routes, network delay, course schedules and build orders.

sections.heading: Dijkstra's idea
sections.body: Always expand the unvisited node with the smallest known distance, using a min-heap. When you pop a node, its distance is final (this requires non-negative weights). Time is O((V + E) log V).
bullets: Push (distance, node) tuples.
Skip stale heap entries if the popped distance is larger than the best known.

sections.heading: When Dijkstra fails
sections.body: Negative edge weights break the final-distance guarantee. Use Bellman-Ford for negative edges (it also detects negative cycles) and BFS for unweighted graphs.
bullets: 0-1 BFS handles edges with weights 0 or 1 using a deque.

sections.heading: Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm)
sections.body: A topological order exists only for a directed acyclic graph. Count the incoming edges of each node, start with nodes that have zero, and repeatedly remove a node and reduce the counts of its neighbors.
bullets: If you cannot place every node, there is a cycle.

sections.heading: Worked example: course schedule
sections.body: Courses are nodes and prerequisites are edges. If Kahn's algorithm outputs all courses, they can all be finished. If it stops early, there is a circular dependency and the answer is False.

sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Network Delay Time (Medium)

mistakes: Using Dijkstra with negative weights.
Not skipping stale heap entries (works but slower).
Treating a graph with a cycle as if it had a topological order.
takeaways: Dijkstra = greedy with a min-heap on non-negative weights.
Kahn's algorithm peels off nodes with zero incoming edges.
Output shorter than n means a cycle.

title: Union-Find and Trie
summary: Track connected groups with DSU and store words by prefix with a trie.
why: These are two specialist structures that make hard problems easy: DSU answers 'are these connected?' almost instantly, and a trie answers prefix questions faster than scanning words.

sections.heading: Union-Find (DSU)
sections.body: Each group is a tree with one representative (root). find(x) follows parents to the root, union(a, b) joins two roots. Path compression and union by size make operations almost O(1), formally O(alpha(n)).
bullets: Use it for connected components, redundant connections and Kruskal's MST.
Union returns False if both nodes were already connected: that edge makes a cycle.

sections.heading: Why it beats DFS here
sections.body: When edges arrive one by one, DFS must rerun from scratch, but DSU updates the groups in near constant time per edge. It is the right tool for dynamic connectivity.

sections.heading: Trie
sections.body: A trie stores words as paths of characters. Insert, search and prefix check each cost O(length of the word), independent of how many words are stored. Mark the end of a word with a flag.
bullets: Autocomplete, spell check and word search II use it.
A dict per node is the simplest Python implementation.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Insert 'apple' and 'app'. search('app') is True, search('ap') is False (not a word), but starts_with('ap') is True. With edges (0,1), (1,2), (0,2) in DSU, the third edge closes a cycle and union returns False.

sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Number of Provinces (Medium)

mistakes: Forgetting path compression, which makes find slow.
Calling union on non-roots instead of find results.
Confusing 'is a prefix' with 'is a word' in a trie.
takeaways: DSU tracks groups; union returning False reveals a cycle.
Path compression plus union by size is near O(1).
A trie makes prefix questions O(word length).

title: Dynamic programming: 1D problems
summary: Break a problem into overlapping subproblems and solve each only once.
why: DP has a scary reputation, but it is a method: define the state, write the transition, set the base case, then optimize. Once you see the method, climbing stairs, house robber and coin change feel alike.

sections.heading: When DP applies
sections.body: Use DP when a problem has overlapping subproblems (the same smaller question appears again) and optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best answers of smaller parts). Words like 'minimum', 'maximum', 'number of ways' are hints.
bullets: If brute force recursion repeats work, think DP.

sections.heading: The four-step method
sections.body: 1) Define dp[i] in plain words. 2) Write how dp[i] depends on smaller states. 3) Set base cases. 4) Decide the order (top-down with memo, or bottom-up with a table).
bullets: Top-down is easier to write; bottom-up is easier to optimize in space.

sections.heading: Classic 1D examples
sections.body: Climbing stairs: ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2). House robber: best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + money[i]). Coin change: fewest(a) = 1 + min(fewest(a - coin)). Longest increasing subsequence has an O(n log n) version using bisect.
bullets: Often you only need the last one or two states, so space becomes O(1).

sections.heading: Worked example: coin change
sections.body: With coins [1, 2, 5] and amount 11, the answer is 3 coins (5 + 5 + 1). Build dp[0..11], where dp[a] is the fewest coins to make a. If no combination exists, return -1.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these in order:
bullets: Climbing Stairs (Easy)
House Robber (Medium)
Coin Change (Medium)
Longest Increasing Subsequence (Medium)
Word Break (Medium)

mistakes: Defining dp[i] vaguely so the transition is unclear.
Forgetting base cases such as dp[0].
Using a greedy approach where only DP is correct.
takeaways: State, transition, base case, order.
Overlapping subproblems plus optimal substructure means DP.
Reduce space when only the last few states matter.

title: DP on grids and strings: knapsack, LCS, edit distance
summary: Fill two-dimensional tables for the most asked DP interview problems.
why: 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence and edit distance are the 'big three' of 2D DP. Their table-filling patterns are reused in dozens of other problems.

sections.heading: 0/1 knapsack
sections.body: Each item can be taken once. dp[w] is the best value with capacity w. Loop capacities from high to low so each item is used at most once. This is O(n * W) time and O(W) space.
bullets: Subset sum and partition equal subset are the same idea with booleans.

sections.heading: Longest common subsequence
sections.body: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of a and first j of b. If characters match, take dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else take the larger of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].
bullets: A subsequence keeps order but may skip characters.

sections.heading: Edit distance
sections.body: dp[i][j] is the fewest edits to turn a[:i] into b[:j]. If characters match, copy the diagonal; otherwise take 1 plus the minimum of insert, delete and replace.
bullets: 'horse' to 'ros' needs 3 edits.

sections.heading: How to read the table
sections.body: Draw the grid on paper, fill the first row and column from base cases, then fill each cell from its neighbors. Writing the table by hand is the fastest way to find a mistake in a transition.

bullets: Unique Paths (Medium)

takeaways: 2D DP: define dp[i][j] in words, then fill from neighbors.
Knapsack loops capacity backward for single-use items.
Draw the table by hand to debug transitions.

title: Greedy algorithms and when they fail
summary: Make the best local choice, and learn how to tell when that is provably enough.
why: Greedy solutions are short and fast, but a greedy idea that looks right can be wrong. Knowing the classic cases and the failure case keeps you safe.

sections.heading: The greedy idea
sections.body: At every step take the choice that looks best now and never reconsider. It works only when a local best is part of a global best, which you justify with an exchange argument: swapping the greedy choice into any optimal answer does not make it worse.
bullets: Greedy usually starts with sorting.

sections.heading: Interval scheduling
sections.body: To attend the most non-overlapping meetings, sort by end time and always take the meeting that finishes first. Sorting by start time fails. 'Minimum removals so none overlap' is the same problem with the answer n minus the kept count.
bullets: Sort key: end time.

sections.heading: Jump game
sections.body: Track the farthest index you can reach. If the current index is beyond the farthest reachable, you are stuck. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.heading: A greedy trap: coin change
sections.body: With coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy picks 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), but 3 + 3 uses 2. Greedy coin change is correct only for special coin systems like 1, 5, 10, 25. In general use DP.
bullets: Always test greedy ideas on small counterexamples.

Trusting greedy without testing a counterexample.

takeaways: Greedy needs a reason, usually an exchange argument.
Sort by end time for interval scheduling.
If a greedy idea has a counterexample, use DP.

title: Bit manipulation
summary: Use AND, OR, XOR and shifts for fast tricks and compact subset enumeration.
why: Bit tricks are short, fast and show up in 'find the single number', 'count set bits' and subset-enumeration questions. A few identities cover most interviews.

sections.heading: The operators
sections.body: & keeps bits that are 1 in both, | keeps bits that are 1 in either, ^ (XOR) keeps bits that differ, ~ flips bits, << multiplies by 2 and >> divides by 2 (integer).
bullets: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x.
x << k equals x * 2^k.

sections.heading: Everyday tricks
sections.body: Check bit i with (x >> i) & 1. Set it with x | (1 << i). Clear it with x & ~(1 << i). A positive number is a power of two when x & (x - 1) == 0, because that expression removes the lowest set bit.
bullets: Brian Kernighan: repeat x &= x - 1 to count set bits.

sections.heading: XOR for the single number
sections.body: If every number appears twice except one, XOR of all numbers cancels the pairs and leaves the single one. O(n) time and O(1) space.

sections.heading: Subsets with bitmasks
sections.body: A set of n items can be encoded as an n-bit number: bit i says whether item i is included. Loop mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 to enumerate all subsets without recursion.
bullets: Bitmask DP builds on this idea.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Single Number (Easy)
Number of 1 Bits (Easy)
Power of Two (Easy)
Counting Bits (Easy)
Missing Number (Easy)

code:
def is_power_of_two(x):
    return x > 0 and x & (x - 1) == 0


def count_set_bits(x):
    count = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1            # remove the lowest set bit
        count += 1
    return count


def single_number(nums):
    result = 0
    for x in nums:
        result ^= x           # pairs cancel out
    return result


def all_subsets(items):
    n = len(items)
    return [[items[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1] for mask in range(1 << n)]


assert is_power_of_two(16) and not is_power_of_two(18) and not is_power_of_two(0)
assert count_set_bits(11) == 3 == bin(11).count("1")
assert single_number([4, 1, 2, 1, 2]) == 4
assert len(all_subsets(["a", "b", "c"])) == 8 and all_subsets(["a", "b"]) == [[], ["a"], ["b"], ["a", "b"]]
x = 0b1010
assert (x >> 1) & 1 == 1 and x | (1 << 2) == 0b1110 and x & ~(1 << 1) == 0b1000
print(bin(count_set_bits(255)))   # 0b1000
mistakes: Forgetting operator precedence: use brackets around shifts and ands.
Treating 0 as a power of two.
Using bit tricks where plain code is clearer and fast enough.
takeaways: x & (x - 1) removes the lowest set bit.
XOR cancels equal numbers.
A bitmask represents a subset.

title: Math for interviews: GCD, primes and modular arithmetic
summary: Use gcd, sieve, fast exponentiation and modular inverse in coding rounds.
why: Many online assessments include one math problem. The same four tools (gcd, sieve, fast power, modulus) cover most of them.

sections.heading: GCD and LCM
sections.body: Euclid's algorithm computes gcd(a, b) by repeatedly replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is 0. It runs in O(log min(a, b)). Then lcm(a, b) = a * b // gcd(a, b).
bullets: Python has math.gcd and math.lcm.

sections.heading: Sieve of Eratosthenes
sections.body: To list all primes up to n, mark multiples of each prime as not prime. It runs in about O(n log log n), far better than testing every number separately.
bullets: Start crossing out from p * p.
Primality for a single number: test divisors up to sqrt(n).

sections.heading: Fast exponentiation and modulus
sections.body: Computing a^b directly can be astronomically large. Square-and-multiply does it in O(log b), and taking the answer modulo m (usually 10^9 + 7) keeps numbers small. Python's pow(a, b, m) already does this.

sections.heading: nCr modulo a prime
sections.body: Division does not work under a modulus, but when m is prime, the inverse of x is pow(x, m - 2, m) (Fermat's little theorem). So nCr = n! * inverse(r!) * inverse((n-r)!) mod m.
bullets: Precompute factorials for many queries.
