sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Count Primes (Medium)
Pow(x, n) (Medium)
Greatest Common Divisor of Strings (Easy)
Unique Paths (Medium, also solvable with nCr)

mistakes: Computing a**b fully and then taking the modulus.
Dividing under a modulus instead of multiplying by the inverse.
Starting the sieve inner loop at 2p instead of p*p (correct but slower).
takeaways: Euclid's algorithm gives gcd in O(log n).
pow(a, b, m) is fast exponentiation.
Under a prime modulus, divide by multiplying with pow(x, m-2, m).

title: DSA pattern cheat sheet: which technique to use
summary: Match problem keywords and input limits to the right pattern in seconds.
why: Strong candidates do not invent a solution from nothing. They recognise the pattern in the first minute. This lesson is the map you keep beside your problem log.

sections.heading: Keywords to patterns
sections.body: Sorted array and pair: two pointers. Longest or shortest subarray or substring: sliding window. Have I seen this: hash set or map. Minimum value that works: binary search on the answer. All combinations or permutations: backtracking. Next greater: monotonic stack. K largest: heap. Shortest path: BFS or Dijkstra. Dependencies: topological sort. Connected groups: DSU. Count ways or optimize with overlap: DP.
bullets: Write the pattern name in your problem log every time.

sections.heading: Input limit to complexity
sections.body: n <= 12 allows O(n!), n <= 25 allows O(2^n), n <= 500 allows O(n^3), n <= 5000 allows O(n^2), n <= 10^6 needs O(n log n), n <= 10^8 needs O(n). If the limit is huge, think math, binary search or O(1).
bullets: A time limit of about 1 second allows about 10^8 simple operations in C++, and far fewer in Python.

sections.heading: Brute force first
sections.body: Always state the brute force and its complexity, then ask what is repeated or wasted. The answer to that question usually names the pattern: repeated lookups mean hashing, repeated range sums mean prefix sums, repeated work on overlapping states means DP.

sections.heading: Build your own sheet
sections.body: After each problem write: pattern, key insight in one line, mistake made, and review date. After 100 problems this sheet is worth more than any book.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Classify before solving:
bullets: Pick 10 random Medium problems and name the pattern in 2 minutes before coding.
Redo your three weakest patterns weekly.

code:
PATTERNS = {
    "sorted pair": "two pointers",
    "longest substring": "sliding window",
    "shortest subarray": "sliding window",
    "seen before": "hash map or set",
    "minimum value such that": "binary search on the answer",
    "all combinations": "backtracking",
    "next greater": "monotonic stack",
    "k largest": "heap",
    "shortest path": "bfs or dijkstra",
    "dependencies": "topological sort",
    "connected groups": "union-find",
    "number of ways": "dynamic programming",
}


def suggest_pattern(problem_text):
    text = problem_text.lower()
    return [p for key, p in PATTERNS.items() if key in text] or ["start with brute force"]


def allowed_complexity(n):
    if n <= 12: return "O(n!)"
    if n <= 25: return "O(2^n)"
    if n <= 500: return "O(n^3)"
    if n <= 5000: return "O(n^2)"
    if n <= 10**6: return "O(n log n)"
    if n <= 10**8: return "O(n)"
    return "O(log n) or O(1)"


assert suggest_pattern("Find the longest substring without repeats") == ["sliding window"]
assert suggest_pattern("Return the k largest values") == ["heap"]
assert suggest_pattern("something unfamiliar") == ["start with brute force"]
assert allowed_complexity(10) == "O(n!)" and allowed_complexity(10**5) == "O(n log n)"
print(allowed_complexity(200000))   # O(n log n)
mistakes: Starting to code before naming the pattern.
Memorizing solutions instead of the trigger words.
Ignoring constraints.
takeaways: Keywords and input limits point to the pattern.
State the brute force, then find the repeated work.
A personal pattern log beats memorizing solutions.

title: The coding interview framework and stress testing
summary: Follow a repeatable routine in interviews and use random tests to catch bugs before the interviewer does.
why: Interviewers score communication and testing as much as the final code. A fixed routine keeps you calm and makes your thinking visible.

sections.heading: The seven steps
sections.body: 1) Repeat the problem in your own words. 2) Ask about input size, duplicates, negatives and empty input. 3) Work a small example by hand. 4) State the brute force and its complexity. 5) Improve it and say the new complexity. 6) Code cleanly. 7) Test with normal, edge and tricky cases, tracing your code.
bullets: Think aloud, but do not narrate every keystroke.

sections.heading: If you are stuck
sections.body: Say what you tried and why it failed. Try a smaller example, a different data structure, or the brute force first. Interviewers help candidates who communicate and rarely help candidates who go silent.

sections.heading: Stress testing
sections.body: Write a slow but obviously correct solution and compare it with your fast solution on thousands of random small inputs. Any mismatch gives you a tiny failing test to debug. This is how competitive programmers find bugs fast.
bullets: Keep inputs small so failures are easy to read.

sections.heading: Online assessment strategy
sections.body: Read all problems first, solve the easiest one fully, then attempt the others. Partial credit matters, so submit a correct brute force if the optimal idea is not coming. Keep a few minutes at the end to re-read the edge cases.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Habits to build:
bullets: Record yourself solving one problem aloud each Saturday.
Write a brute force and stress test for every Medium you solve this week.

code:
import random


def max_subarray_brute(nums):
    """Slow but obviously correct: O(n^2)."""
    best = nums[0]
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, len(nums)):
            total += nums[j]
            best = max(best, total)
    return best


def max_subarray_fast(nums):
    """Kadane: O(n)."""
    best = cur = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best


def stress_test(fast, brute, trials=2000):
    for _ in range(trials):
        data = [random.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
        if fast(data) != brute(data):
            return data                      # smallest failing example to debug
    return None


assert stress_test(max_subarray_fast, max_subarray_brute) is None


def buggy(nums):                             # forgets all-negative arrays
    best = cur = 0
    for x in nums:
        cur = max(0, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best


failing = stress_test(buggy, max_subarray_brute)
assert failing is not None                   # stress testing finds the bug
print("bug found on input:", failing)
mistakes: Coding before clarifying the problem.
Going silent when stuck.
Testing only the sample input.
takeaways: A fixed routine keeps your thinking visible.
Brute force first, then optimize.
Stress testing against a brute force finds hidden bugs.

title: OOP in Python: classes, dunder methods and dataclasses
summary: Model real things with classes, inheritance, properties and dataclasses.
why: Python developer interviews always include OOP. You must explain the four pillars, show them in code, and know the Python-specific tools: dunder methods, properties, dataclasses and the method resolution order.

sections.heading: Classes and the four pillars
sections.body: Encapsulation keeps data and the code that uses it together. Abstraction hides details behind a simple interface. Inheritance reuses behavior in a subclass. Polymorphism lets different classes answer the same method call in their own way.
bullets: Python uses a leading underscore (_name) as a convention for 'internal'.
Prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) when unsure.

sections.heading: Dunder methods
sections.body: Special methods let your objects behave like built-in types. __repr__ gives a debug string, __eq__ defines equality, __hash__ allows use in sets and dict keys, __lt__ allows sorting, __len__ and __iter__ make containers.
bullets: If you define __eq__, also define __hash__ for hashable objects.
__repr__ should be unambiguous; __str__ should be friendly.

sections.heading: Properties and abstract classes
sections.body: @property turns a method into a read-style attribute and lets you validate on assignment without changing the caller's code. An abstract base class (ABC) forces subclasses to implement required methods.
bullets: Raise ValueError in a setter for bad values.

sections.heading: Dataclasses and MRO
sections.body: @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you from field annotations. For multiple inheritance Python uses the C3 method resolution order: look in the class, then its parents left to right, with each class appearing once. ClassName.__mro__ shows the order.
bullets: field(default_factory=list) avoids the mutable default trap.
dataclass(order=True) adds comparisons.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Build these from memory:
bullets: A BankAccount with validation, deposit and withdraw.
A Shape ABC with Circle and Rectangle.
A Stack class with __len__ and __iter__.

mistakes: Defining __eq__ without __hash__ and then using the object in sets.
Using a mutable default value in a class or dataclass field.
Deep inheritance trees where composition is simpler.
takeaways: Dunder methods make your objects feel native.
Properties validate without changing how callers use the class.
Dataclasses remove boilerplate; MRO decides method lookup.

title: Iterators and generators
summary: Process large or infinite data lazily with yield and generator pipelines.
why: Generators let you handle files, streams and big datasets without loading everything into memory. They are a favorite Python interview topic and the base of async code.

sections.heading: Iterables and iterators
sections.body: An iterable can give an iterator (iter(x)). An iterator has __next__ and raises StopIteration when finished. A for loop calls iter() once and next() repeatedly. Lists are iterables; they are not iterators.
bullets: An iterator can be consumed only once.

sections.heading: Generator functions
sections.body: A function with yield returns a generator. It pauses at each yield, keeps its local state, and resumes on the next request. Values are produced lazily, one at a time, so memory use stays constant.
bullets: Generator expressions: (x * x for x in data).
Infinite sequences are possible, such as Fibonacci.

sections.heading: Pipelines
sections.body: Chain generators so each stage processes one item at a time. Reading, cleaning and converting a 10 GB log file can use only a few kilobytes of memory.
bullets: Use itertools.islice to take part of an infinite generator.

sections.heading: When not to use them
sections.body: If you need the length, random access or several passes over the data, build a list. Generators are one-pass tools.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Try these:
bullets: Write a generator that yields lines of a file that contain 'ERROR'.
Write a chunking generator that yields batches of size n.
Explain the difference between return and yield.

mistakes: Trying to reuse a generator after it is exhausted.
Converting a generator to a list and losing the memory benefit.
Forgetting that the code inside a generator does not run until it is iterated.
takeaways: yield pauses and resumes a function with its state.
Generators are lazy and use constant memory.
Pipelines of generators process one item at a time.

title: Decorators and context managers
summary: Wrap behavior around functions and manage resources with with statements.
why: Frameworks like Flask, FastAPI and pytest are built on decorators and context managers. Understanding them turns magic syntax into ordinary Python.

sections.heading: Functions are objects
sections.body: In Python you can pass a function to another function and return a new function. A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns an improved version. @decorator is only shorthand for func = decorator(func).
bullets: A closure remembers variables from the enclosing scope.

sections.heading: A correct decorator
sections.body: Use *args and **kwargs so the wrapper accepts any call, and use functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring. For decorators with arguments, add one more outer function (a decorator factory).
bullets: Common uses: timing, caching, retry, authentication, logging.

sections.heading: Context managers
sections.body: The with statement guarantees cleanup. A class needs __enter__ and __exit__. The easier way is @contextmanager from contextlib: code before yield is setup, code after (inside finally) is cleanup.
bullets: Use for files, locks, database connections and temporary settings.

sections.heading: Worked example: retry
sections.body: retry(times=3) wraps a flaky function, calls it again after a failure, and re-raises the last error if all attempts fail. The same pattern is used for network calls.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Try these:
bullets: Write a decorator that caches results (then compare with functools.cache).
Write a timer context manager.
Explain what @wraps fixes.

mistakes: Forgetting functools.wraps, which loses the function name.
Not returning the wrapped function's result.
Putting cleanup outside try/finally in a context manager.
takeaways: @decorator means func = decorator(func).
Use wraps, *args and **kwargs in every wrapper.
Context managers guarantee cleanup even on errors.

title: Threads, processes, the GIL and asyncio
summary: Choose the right concurrency tool for I/O-bound and CPU-bound work.
why: Interviewers love 'What is the GIL?' and 'threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio'. Knowing the difference also helps you build faster APIs and scrapers.

sections.heading: I/O-bound versus CPU-bound
sections.body: I/O-bound code spends time waiting (network, disk, database). CPU-bound code spends time calculating. The right tool depends on which one you have.
bullets: Waiting work: threads or asyncio.
Calculating work: multiprocessing.

sections.heading: The GIL
sections.body: CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock: only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help with I/O because the lock is released while waiting, but they do not speed up pure CPU work. Multiprocessing uses separate processes, each with its own GIL.
bullets: Recent Python versions have experimental free-threaded builds, but the GIL remains the default.
NumPy releases the GIL in many operations.

sections.heading: Threads and locks
sections.body: ThreadPoolExecutor runs I/O tasks in parallel. Threads share memory, so updating shared data needs a Lock to avoid race conditions. Keep locked sections tiny.
bullets: A race condition is a bug that appears only under unlucky timing.

sections.heading: asyncio
sections.body: asyncio runs many tasks on one thread. A task gives control back at each await, so thousands of waiting tasks fit in a single thread. Everything on the path must be non-blocking: time.sleep blocks the loop, asyncio.sleep does not.
bullets: asyncio.gather runs coroutines together.
async def does not make code fast by itself.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Try these:
bullets: Download 20 URLs with a thread pool, then with asyncio.
Compute primes in a process pool.
Explain a race condition and fix it with a Lock.

code:
import asyncio
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def io_task(_):
    time.sleep(0.05)               # pretend: wait for a network reply
    return "done"


async def async_io_task(_):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)      # non-blocking wait
    return "done"


async def run_async(n):
    return await asyncio.gather(*(async_io_task(i) for i in range(n)))


# 1) Sequential: waits add up
start = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(5):
    io_task(i)
sequential = time.perf_counter() - start

# 2) Threads: waits overlap
start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(io_task, range(5)))
threaded = time.perf_counter() - start

# 3) asyncio: waits overlap on ONE thread
start = time.perf_counter()
async_results = asyncio.run(run_async(5))
async_time = time.perf_counter() - start

assert results == async_results == ["done"] * 5
assert threaded < sequential * 0.7 and async_time < sequential * 0.7

# 4) Shared data needs a lock
counter, lock = 0, threading.Lock()


def increment(times):
    global counter
    for _ in range(times):
        with lock:                 # remove the lock and updates can be lost
            counter += 1


workers = [threading.Thread(target=increment, args=(10000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for w in workers: w.start()
for w in workers: w.join()
assert counter == 40000
print(f"sequential {sequential:.2f}s, threads {threaded:.2f}s, asyncio {async_time:.2f}s")
mistakes: Using threads to speed up CPU-bound Python code.
Calling a blocking function (time.sleep, requests.get) inside async code.
Sharing mutable state between threads without a lock.
takeaways: GIL: one thread runs Python bytecode at a time.
I/O-bound: threads or asyncio. CPU-bound: processes.
Protect shared state with locks.

title: REST API design: methods, status codes and idempotency
summary: Design clean HTTP APIs and understand the rules behind FastAPI, Flask and Django REST.
why: Backend interviews check whether you understand what an API promises: which method to use, which status code to return, and what happens on retry. The framework is less important than these rules.

sections.heading: Resources and methods
sections.body: Name URLs after things (nouns), not actions: /users and /users/42. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes. GET must never change data.
bullets: Use plural nouns.
Version your API: /api/v1/users.

sections.heading: Status codes that matter
sections.body: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request (invalid input), 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (logged in but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Server Error.
bullets: 4xx means the client made a mistake; 5xx means the server did.

sections.heading: Idempotency
sections.body: An operation is idempotent if repeating it gives the same final state. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, so a retried POST can create duplicates. Payment APIs fix this with idempotency keys.
bullets: Safe retries are essential for unreliable networks.

sections.heading: Validation, pagination and errors
sections.body: Validate input at the edge (Pydantic does this in FastAPI). Never return unlimited lists: use limit and offset or a cursor. Return errors in a consistent JSON shape with a message the client can show.
bullets: Authenticate with tokens (JWT or sessions) and hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Build these:
bullets: A users API with create, read, update, delete and pagination.
Add JWT login to it.
Write tests that check each status code.

mistakes: Using verbs in URLs, like /getUsers.
Returning 200 with an error message inside.
Confusing 401 (who are you?) with 403 (you may not).
takeaways: Nouns in URLs; the HTTP method is the verb.
Pick the correct status code every time.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

title: SQL queries you must know
summary: Practice joins, group by, window functions and safe parameterized queries with a real database.
why: SQL appears in almost every placement process, either as MCQs or as live query writing. Running the queries below yourself with sqlite3 is the fastest way to learn.

sections.heading: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING
sections.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Aggregates are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
bullets: Use COUNT(*) to count rows.
Remember NULL: use IS NULL, not = NULL.

sections.heading: Joins
sections.body: INNER JOIN keeps rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills NULL when there is no match, which is how you find 'departments with no employees'.
bullets: Use table aliases to keep queries short.

sections.heading: Classic interview queries
sections.body: Second highest salary: SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1. Duplicates: GROUP BY the column and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Top per group: use a window function such as DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC).
bullets: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ in how they handle ties.

sections.heading: Parameterized queries stop SQL injection
sections.body: Never build SQL by joining strings with user input. Pass values with ? placeholders so the database treats them as data, never as code.
bullets: ORMs such as SQLAlchemy do this for you.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Solve these on a sample table:
bullets: Nth highest salary.
Employees earning more than their department average.
Departments with zero employees.
Running total of salaries.

code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE depts (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);
INSERT INTO depts VALUES ('IT'), ('HR'), ('Sales'), ('Legal');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES
  (1, 'Asha', 'IT', 90), (2, 'Ravi', 'IT', 70), (3, 'Meena', 'HR', 60),
  (4, 'John', 'HR', 60), (5, 'Kiran', 'Sales', 80);
""")


def q(sql, params=()):
    return con.execute(sql, params).fetchall()


# highest salary per department
assert q("SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept") == [("HR", 60), ("IT", 90), ("Sales", 80)]

# second highest distinct salary
assert q("SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1") == [(80,)]

# duplicate salaries
assert q("SELECT salary, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*) > 1") == [(60, 2)]

# LEFT JOIN: departments with no employees
assert q("""SELECT d.name FROM depts d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept = d.name
            WHERE e.id IS NULL""") == [("Legal",)]

# window function: rank inside each department
ranked = q("""SELECT name, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
              FROM employees ORDER BY dept, r, name""")
assert ranked == [("John", 1), ("Meena", 1), ("Asha", 1), ("Ravi", 2), ("Kiran", 1)]

# safe parameter versus injection attempt
evil = "x' OR '1'='1"
assert q("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name = ?", (evil,)) == []
print(q("SELECT dept, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept"))
mistakes: Using WHERE where HAVING is needed (filtering aggregates).
Comparing with = NULL.
Building SQL strings with f-strings and user input.
takeaways: Know the logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds missing matches.
Always use parameterized queries.

title: Operating systems: scheduling and deadlock
summary: Simulate round-robin scheduling and detect deadlock with the Banker's algorithm and wait-for graphs.
why: OS is asked in almost every campus interview. These two topics (CPU scheduling and deadlock) are the most common numerical and conceptual questions.

sections.heading: Process, thread, context switch
sections.body: A process is a running program with its own memory. A thread is a lightweight path of execution inside a process that shares its memory. A context switch saves one task's state and loads another's, which costs time but lets the CPU stay busy.
bullets: Process states: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.

sections.heading: CPU scheduling
sections.body: FCFS is simple but short jobs wait behind long ones. SJF minimizes average waiting time but needs burst estimates and can starve long jobs. Round robin gives each process a time quantum in turn, which is fair and good for interactive systems. Priority scheduling can starve low priority jobs unless aging is used.
bullets: Turnaround time = completion - arrival.
Waiting time = turnaround - burst.

sections.heading: Deadlock
sections.body: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break any one to prevent deadlock. Detect it by finding a cycle in the wait-for graph. The Banker's algorithm avoids it by granting a request only if the system stays in a safe state.
bullets: Safe state means some order lets every process finish.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Three processes (P1 arrives 0 burst 5, P2 arrives 1 burst 3, P3 arrives 2 burst 1) with quantum 2 finish at times P3 = 5, P2 = 8, P1 = 9. Waiting times are 4, 4 and 2. Run the code to see it.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Draw the Gantt chart for FCFS, SJF and RR on the same input.
Check a Banker's safe sequence by hand.
Explain the dining philosophers problem.

mistakes: Mixing up turnaround time and waiting time.
Forgetting that new arrivals join the queue before the preempted process.
Saying an unsafe state is always a deadlock (it only may lead to one).
takeaways: Round robin is fair; SJF minimizes waiting but can starve.
Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions.
Banker's algorithm grants only requests that keep the state safe.

title: DBMS: ACID, normalization and indexing
summary: Understand transactions, why tables are normalized, and how an index speeds up queries.
why: DBMS theory (ACID, normal forms, indexes, isolation) is a guaranteed interview topic. Seeing a rollback and a query plan on a real database makes the theory stick.

sections.heading: ACID
sections.body: Atomicity: all steps of a transaction happen or none do. Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another (constraints hold). Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.
bullets: Classic example: money transfer between two accounts.

sections.heading: Normalization
sections.body: 1NF: every cell holds one atomic value. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a composite key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key. Normalizing removes redundancy and update anomalies, while denormalizing trades that for read speed.
bullets: Insert, update and delete anomalies are the problems normalization solves.

sections.heading: Indexes
sections.body: An index (usually a B+ tree) lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table: O(log n) instead of O(n). Indexes speed up reads on the indexed columns but slow down writes and use space, so index columns you filter, join or sort by.
bullets: A composite index follows the leftmost-prefix rule.
Primary keys are indexed automatically.

sections.heading: Isolation levels
sections.body: Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed prevents dirty reads. Repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable prevents phantom reads too, at the highest cost. Choose the weakest level that keeps your data correct.
bullets: Deadlocks in databases are detected and one transaction is rolled back.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Normalize a messy orders table to 3NF.
Explain when an index will not be used.
Write a transfer function with rollback.

mistakes: Thinking normalization always improves speed (it improves consistency; reads may need joins).
Indexing every column, which slows writes.
Confusing consistency in ACID with consistency in the CAP theorem.
takeaways: ACID: all-or-nothing, valid, isolated, durable.
Normal forms remove redundancy and anomalies.
Indexes speed reads and cost writes and space.

title: Computer networks: what happens when you type a URL
summary: Follow a request through DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP, and learn subnetting basics.
why: 'What happens when you type google.com and press Enter?' is the most famous networking question. A clear step-by-step answer shows you understand the whole stack.

sections.heading: The journey of a request
sections.body: 1) The browser checks its cache. 2) DNS turns the domain into an IP address. 3) TCP connects with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). 4) For HTTPS, TLS negotiates encryption. 5) The browser sends an HTTP request. 6) The server replies with a status code and content. 7) The browser renders the page, fetching more resources.
bullets: Each layer solves one problem: DNS names, TCP reliability, TLS security, HTTP content.

sections.heading: TCP versus UDP
sections.body: TCP is connection-based and reliable: it orders data, retransmits lost packets and controls congestion. UDP is connectionless and fast with no guarantees. Use TCP for web, email and file transfer; UDP for live video, games and DNS queries.
bullets: OSI layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.

sections.heading: HTTP essentials
sections.body: A request has a method, path, headers and optional body. A response has a status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers and a body. HTTP is stateless, so cookies, sessions or tokens carry login state. HTTPS adds TLS encryption and server identity.
bullets: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP).

sections.heading: IP addresses and subnets
sections.body: An IPv4 address has 32 bits. A prefix such as /24 says the first 24 bits identify the network, leaving 8 bits (256 addresses, 254 usable hosts) for devices. Splitting a /24 into four /26 networks gives 64 addresses each. NAT lets many private devices share one public IP.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Write the 7-step answer to 'what happens when you type a URL' from memory.
Calculate hosts per subnet for /26, /27 and /28.
Explain ARP, DHCP and NAT in two lines each.

from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlparse

url = "https://shop.example.com:8443/products?id=42&sort=price#reviews"
parts = urlparse(url)
assert (parts.scheme, parts.hostname, parts.port) == ("https", "shop.example.com", 8443)
assert parts.path == "/products" and parts.fragment == "reviews"
assert parse_qs(parts.query) == {"id": ["42"], "sort": ["price"]}


def build_request(method, host, path):
    return f"{method} {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"


def parse_status_line(line):
    version, code, reason = line.split(" ", 2)
    return version, int(code), reason


request = build_request("GET", "example.com", "/index.html")
assert request.startswith("GET /index.html HTTP/1.1") and request.endswith("\r\n\r\n")
assert parse_status_line("HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found") == ("HTTP/1.1", 404, "Not Found")


class DnsCache:
    """A resolver cache with a time-to-live (TTL)."""

    def __init__(self, clock):
        self.clock, self.entries = clock, {}

    def put(self, name, ip, ttl):
        self.entries[name] = (ip, self.clock() + ttl)

    def get(self, name):
        ip, expires = self.entries.get(name, (None, 0))
        return ip if self.clock() < expires else None


now = [0]
cache = DnsCache(lambda: now[0])
cache.put("example.com", "93.184.216.34", ttl=60)
assert cache.get("example.com") == "93.184.216.34"
now[0] = 61
assert cache.get("example.com") is None              # expired, must ask DNS again

network = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.10.0/24")
assert network.num_addresses == 256 and len(list(network.hosts())) == 254
assert str(network.broadcast_address) == "192.168.10.255"
subnets = list(network.subnets(new_prefix=26))
assert len(subnets) == 4 and subnets[0].num_addresses == 64
assert ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.10.77") in subnets[1]
print([str(s) for s in subnets])
mistakes: Saying HTTP is encrypted (HTTPS adds TLS).
Forgetting DNS in the URL journey.
Counting all addresses as usable hosts (network and broadcast are reserved).
takeaways: URL journey: cache, DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, render.
TCP is reliable; UDP is fast.
A /n prefix leaves 32-n host bits.

title: Low-level design: LRU cache and rate limiter
summary: Design two classic components with clear classes, tests and trade-offs.
why: LLD rounds ask you to design small systems with clean classes. LRU cache and rate limiter are the two most common, and they combine data structures with real engineering judgment.

sections.heading: How to answer an LLD question
sections.body: 1) Clarify requirements and limits. 2) List the operations (the public API). 3) Choose the data structures. 4) Write the classes with small responsibilities. 5) Test normal and edge cases. 6) Discuss extensions: thread safety, persistence, distribution.
bullets: Make time and randomness injectable so tests are easy.

sections.heading: LRU cache
sections.body: Least Recently Used evicts the item unused for the longest time when the cache is full. You need O(1) get and put, so combine a hash map (find fast) with a doubly linked list (move to front and remove from the back fast). Python's OrderedDict already does both.
bullets: get marks an item as recently used.
put on an existing key updates and refreshes it.

sections.heading: Token bucket rate limiter
sections.body: A bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request spends one token; with no tokens the request is rejected (HTTP 429). It allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate. Compute the refill lazily on each request instead of running a timer.
bullets: Alternatives: fixed window (simple, edge bursts), sliding window (accurate, more memory).

sections.heading: Production notes
sections.body: Add a lock for multi-threaded use. For many servers, keep counters in Redis. Return a Retry-After header so clients can back off.
bullets: Say what you would monitor: hit rate, rejections, latency.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Design next:
bullets: Parking lot
Elevator controller
Tic-tac-toe
LFU cache

code:
from collections import OrderedDict


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity, self.data = capacity, OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return -1
        self.data.move_to_end(key)             # most recently used goes last
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.data:
            self.data.move_to_end(key)
        self.data[key] = value
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)      # evict the least recently used


class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_sec, clock):
        self.capacity, self.rate, self.clock = capacity, refill_per_sec, clock
        self.tokens, self.last = capacity, clock()

    def allow(self):
        now = self.clock()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False


cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put("a", 1); cache.put("b", 2)
assert cache.get("a") == 1                    # a is now most recent
cache.put("c", 3)                             # evicts b
assert cache.get("b") == -1 and cache.get("a") == 1 and cache.get("c") == 3
cache.put("a", 10)
assert cache.get("a") == 10

fake_time = [0.0]
bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=2, refill_per_sec=1, clock=lambda: fake_time[0])
assert bucket.allow() and bucket.allow()      # burst of 2
assert not bucket.allow()                     # empty
fake_time[0] = 1.0
assert bucket.allow() and not bucket.allow()  # one token refilled
fake_time[0] = 100.0
assert bucket.allow() and bucket.allow() and not bucket.allow()   # capped at capacity
print("LRU and token bucket checks passed")
mistakes: Using a plain dict plus a list and getting O(n) updates.
Running a timer thread for token refill instead of computing it lazily.
Not injecting the clock, which makes tests slow and flaky.
takeaways: LRU = hash map plus ordering, both O(1).
Token bucket allows bursts but limits the average rate.
Inject time so the design is testable.

title: Percentages, profit and loss, discount
summary: Master the formulas and shortcuts that appear in every aptitude test.
why: Percentage-based questions are the largest group in quantitative aptitude. They also sit inside profit, discount, interest and data interpretation, so one strong foundation pays off in many places.

sections.heading: Percentage basics
sections.body: x% of y is x * y / 100. Percentage change is (new - old) / old * 100, always measured against the old value. Successive changes of a% and b% give a net change of a + b + ab/100 percent.
bullets: A rise of 20% followed by a fall of 20% is a net fall of 4%, not 0.
To increase by 20%, multiply by 1.2; to decrease by 20%, multiply by 0.8.

sections.heading: Profit, loss and discount
sections.body: Profit% = (SP - CP) / CP * 100 and loss% is measured on the cost price too. Discount is on the marked price (MP): SP = MP * (1 - d/100). Profit and discount are different bases, which is where most mistakes happen.
bullets: Two successive discounts a% and b% equal a + b - ab/100 percent.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.body: 1) CP 500, SP 600: profit = 100 / 500 = 20%. 2) MP 1000 with 20% discount gives SP 800. If this is a 10% profit then CP = 800 / 1.1 = 727.27. 3) Price 100 up 20% then down 20% = 96, a net 4% fall.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 20 percentage questions in 20 minutes.
10 profit and loss questions with discount.
Convert 15 fractions to percentages without a calculator.

mistakes: Calculating percentage change on the new value instead of the old.
Using the marked price as the base for profit.
Treating a +20% then -20% change as zero.
takeaways: Change is always measured against the old value.
Successive changes multiply: a + b + ab/100.
Profit is on CP; discount is on MP.

title: Ratio, averages and alligation
summary: Split quantities by ratio, handle averages smartly and solve mixture questions with alligation.
why: Ratio and average ideas are used in ages, partnership, mixtures, work and speed. Alligation especially saves minutes in mixture questions.

sections.heading: Ratio and proportion
sections.body: A ratio a : b compares two quantities. To split T in the ratio a : b : c, give each part T * a / (a + b + c) and so on. If a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, make b the same in both (12, the LCM of 3 and 4) to get a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15.
bullets: Keep the common term equal before joining ratios.
Ratios have no units.

sections.heading: Averages
sections.body: Average = sum / count, so sum = average * count. If a value leaves the group, the new sum is the old sum minus that value. A weighted average multiplies each average by the group size.
bullets: Average of consecutive numbers is the middle number.
Adding a number above the average raises it; below, lowers it.

sections.heading: Alligation
sections.body: To mix two items with values cheaper (c) and dearer (d) to get mean m, the ratio of cheaper to dearer quantity is (d - m) : (m - c). It is the cross-difference of the three values, with no equations needed.
bullets: Works for prices, concentrations and averages.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.body: 1) Split 750 in 2 : 3 : 5 gives 150, 225, 375. 2) Average of 5 numbers is 20. After removing one number the average of the rest is 18, so the removed number is 100 - 72 = 28. 3) Mix 30% and 50% solutions to get 42%: ratio (50-42) : (42-30) = 8 : 12 = 2 : 3.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 10 ratio-sharing questions.
10 'average changes when one item is replaced' questions.
10 alligation questions.

mistakes: Joining ratios without making the common term equal.
Reversing the order in alligation.
Averaging two averages without weighting by group size.
takeaways: Split by parts: total * part / sum of parts.
sum = average * count solves most average puzzles.
Alligation = cross-difference of dearer, mean and cheaper.

title: Time and work, speed and distance, trains and boats
summary: Convert word problems into rates and solve them with a handful of formulas.
why: Time-work and time-speed-distance (TSD) questions appear in almost every placement test. They look different but are the same rate idea: rate times time equals total.

sections.heading: Work as a rate
sections.body: If A finishes a job in 10 days, A's rate is 1/10 of the job per day. Rates add when people work together: A and B together take 1 / (1/a + 1/b) = ab/(a + b) days. A pipe that empties counts as a negative rate.
bullets: Work = rate * time.
Efficiency ratio is the inverse of the days ratio.

sections.heading: Speed, distance, time
sections.body: distance = speed * time. To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18; for m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5. For equal distances at speeds a and b the average speed is 2ab/(a + b), not (a + b)/2.
bullets: Relative speed: subtract for the same direction, add for opposite.

sections.heading: Trains
sections.body: A train crossing a pole travels its own length. Crossing a platform it travels its length plus the platform length. Two trains crossing each other use the sum of lengths divided by the relative speed.
bullets: Convert units first, then calculate.

sections.heading: Boats and streams
sections.body: Downstream speed = boat + stream; upstream speed = boat - stream. Boat speed = (down + up) / 2 and stream speed = (down - up) / 2.
bullets: Round trips take longer than the same distance in still water.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.body: 1) A in 10 days, B in 15: together 6 days. 2) A 150 m train at 54 km/h = 15 m/s crosses a pole in 10 s. 3) 60 km/h and 40 km/h over equal distances: 48 km/h average. 4) Boat 8 km/h in still water, stream 2 km/h: 30 km downstream takes 3 h, upstream takes 5 h.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 10 time-work questions with pipes.
10 train questions.
10 boats and streams questions.

mistakes: Averaging speeds as (a + b) / 2 for equal distances.
Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s in train problems.
Adding days instead of adding rates.
takeaways: Add rates, not days.
Convert units before calculating.
Equal-distance average speed is 2ab/(a + b).

title: Permutations, combinations and probability
summary: Count arrangements and selections, then turn counts into probabilities.
why: Counting and probability questions reward clear thinking more than formulas. The skill is deciding: does order matter, can items repeat, and which cases are favorable?

sections.heading: Order matters or not
sections.body: Permutation nPr counts ordered arrangements, combination nCr counts selections where order does not matter. nPr = n! / (n - r)! and nCr = n! / (r! (n - r)!). If you pick a team, use nCr; if you assign roles, use nPr.
bullets: n! counts arrangements of n different items.
Circular arrangements of n items: (n - 1)!.

sections.heading: Repeated letters
sections.body: Arrangements of a word with repeats equal n! divided by the factorial of each repeat count. LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice, so 5! / (2! * 2!) = 30.
bullets: Treat identical items as one type.

sections.heading: Probability
sections.body: P(event) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes. For independent events multiply, for either of two exclusive events add. For 'at least one', use 1 minus the probability of none: it is usually much shorter.
bullets: Probability is always between 0 and 1.
Always check that the outcomes you count are equally likely.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.body: 1) Two dice sum to 7: 6 favorable out of 36 = 1/6. 2) Choose 3 from 5 men and 4 women with at least one woman: C(9,3) - C(5,3) = 84 - 10 = 74. 3) At least one head in 3 tosses: 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. 4) Seat 5 people around a table: 4! = 24.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 10 arrangement questions with restrictions.
10 committee questions.

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import permutations, product


def distinct_arrangements(word):
    count = math.factorial(len(word))
    for letter in set(word):
        count //= math.factorial(word.count(letter))
    return count


assert distinct_arrangements("LEVEL") == 30 == len(set(permutations("LEVEL")))   # formula = brute force
assert math.perm(5, 2) == 20 and math.comb(5, 2) == 10

# two dice sum to 7
rolls = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
assert Fraction(sum(1 for a, b in rolls if a + b == 7), len(rolls)) == Fraction(1, 6)

# committee of 3 from 5 men and 4 women with at least one woman
assert math.comb(9, 3) - math.comb(5, 3) == 74

# at least one head in 3 tosses
tosses = list(product("HT", repeat=3))
assert Fraction(sum(1 for t in tosses if "H" in t), len(tosses)) == Fraction(7, 8)

assert math.factorial(5 - 1) == 24                           # circular seating
assert math.comb(10, 2) == 45                                # handshakes among 10 people
print(distinct_arrangements("BALLOON"))   # 1260
mistakes: Using permutations when order does not matter.
Forgetting to divide by repeated-letter factorials.
Adding probabilities of events that can happen together.
takeaways: Ask: does order matter?
'At least one' = 1 minus 'none'.
Verify formulas by brute-force counting on small cases.

title: Number system: divisibility, HCF, LCM and remainders
summary: Use divisibility rules, HCF-LCM identities, unit digits and factor counting quickly.
why: Number-system questions are short and score-friendly if you know the rules. They also feed directly into coding rounds (gcd, primes, modulus).

sections.heading: Divisibility rules
sections.body: By 2: last digit even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 4: last two digits divisible by 4. By 5: ends in 0 or 5. By 8: last three digits divisible by 8. By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: difference between sum of odd-place and even-place digits is 0 or a multiple of 11.
bullets: A number divisible by 2 and 3 is divisible by 6.

sections.heading: HCF and LCM
sections.body: HCF is the largest number dividing all given numbers; LCM is the smallest number divisible by all of them. For two numbers HCF * LCM = product. For 'smallest number leaving remainder r when divided by a, b, c', the answer is LCM(a, b, c) + r.
bullets: Use HCF for splitting into equal groups and LCM for events that repeat together.

sections.heading: Unit digits and trailing zeros
sections.body: Unit digits of powers repeat in cycles of length 4 or less (7 gives 7, 9, 3, 1). So find the exponent modulo 4. Trailing zeros of n! equal n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + ... because each zero needs a pair 2 and 5 and 5s are rarer.
bullets: pow(a, b, 10) gives the unit digit directly in code.

sections.heading: Counting factors
sections.body: Write the number as p^a * q^b * r^c. The count of factors is (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1). 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5 has 4 * 3 * 2 = 24 factors. A number has an odd count of factors only if it is a perfect square.
bullets: Sum of factors uses a similar formula.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 10 remainder questions.
10 HCF/LCM word problems.
10 unit digit and trailing zero questions.

code:
import math


def smallest_with_remainder(r, *divisors):
    return math.lcm(*divisors) + r


def trailing_zeros_factorial(n):
    count, power = 0, 5
    while power <= n:
        count += n // power
        power *= 5
    return count


def factor_count(n):
    count, p = 1, 2
    while p * p <= n:
        exp = 0
        while n % p == 0:
            n //= p
            exp += 1
        count *= exp + 1
        p += 1
    return count * 2 if n > 1 else count


def divisible_by_11(n):
    digits = [int(d) for d in str(n)]
    return (sum(digits[::2]) - sum(digits[1::2])) % 11 == 0


a, b = 12, 18
assert math.gcd(a, b) * math.lcm(a, b) == a * b             # HCF x LCM = product
assert smallest_with_remainder(3, 4, 5, 6) == 63
assert pow(7, 123, 10) == 3                                 # cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 123 mod 4 = 3
assert trailing_zeros_factorial(100) == 24 == len(str(math.factorial(100))) - len(str(math.factorial(100)).rstrip("0"))
assert factor_count(360) == 24
assert divisible_by_11(918082) and not divisible_by_11(123456)
assert factor_count(36) % 2 == 1                            # perfect square: odd number of factors
print(factor_count(360))   # 24
mistakes: Using LCM when HCF is needed (and vice versa).
Forgetting to add the remainder after taking the LCM.
Counting zeros from only the 5s in n/5 and ignoring n/25.
takeaways: HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers.
Cycle of unit digits: use exponent mod 4.
Factor count = product of (exponent + 1).

title: Logical reasoning: series, coding, directions and seating
summary: Solve the most common reasoning question types with systematic methods.
why: Reasoning questions look random, but each type has a method. Practicing the methods turns slow guessing into quick, reliable answers.

sections.heading: Number series
sections.body: Check differences first (arithmetic), then ratios (geometric), then differences of differences (squares and cubes). Also look for alternating series and prime or Fibonacci patterns.
bullets: 2, 6, 18, 54: multiply by 3.
1, 4, 9, 16: differences 3, 5, 7 grow by 2.

sections.heading: Coding-decoding
sections.body: Write the letters with their numbers (A = 1 ... Z = 26). Test a constant shift, a reversed alphabet (A <-> Z) or a position-based shift. Apply the same rule to the new word.
bullets: CAT with a +2 shift becomes ECV.

sections.heading: Blood relations and directions
sections.body: Draw a family tree with generations in rows and mark gender with symbols. For directions, put the start at (0, 0), treat north as +y and east as +x, and compute the final point; the shortest distance is the straight line (Pythagoras).
bullets: Never solve blood relations in your head.

sections.heading: Seating arrangements
sections.body: Fix the most restricted person first, list the constraints, and eliminate arrangements. For small puzzles you can think of it as brute force with pruning: try the possibilities and discard those that break a rule.
bullets: Linear row: positions 1 to n. Circular: fix one person to remove rotation.

sections.body: Do these:
bullets: 15 series questions in 15 minutes.
5 seating puzzles with 5 to 8 people.
10 blood relation questions drawn as trees.

mistakes: Jumping to a complex rule before checking simple differences.
Not drawing the family tree or the diagram.
Starting a seating puzzle with the least restricted person.
takeaways: Series: differences, then ratios, then second differences.
Draw every blood-relation and direction problem.
Start seating puzzles from the most restricted person.

title: Data interpretation and speed maths
summary: Read tables and charts quickly and use calculation shortcuts to save minutes.
why: DI sets are time-consuming because of calculations, not because of difficulty. Speed-maths shortcuts and approximation turn a 6-minute set into a 3-minute set.

sections.heading: Read before you calculate
sections.body: Spend 30 seconds on the title, units, years and axis labels. Many wrong answers come from reading thousands as lakhs or percentages as counts. Only then read the questions and calculate what is needed.
bullets: Tables: find the row and column first.
Pie chart: the whole is 360 degrees or 100%.

sections.heading: The four formulas
sections.body: Percentage change = (new - old) / old * 100. Share = part / total * 100. Ratio = A / B. Average = total / count. Almost every DI question is one of these four with some reading.
bullets: 'Percentage point' difference is a plain subtraction of two percentages.

sections.heading: Calculation shortcuts
sections.body: Squares ending in 5: n5 squared is n(n + 1) followed by 25, so 65 squared is 6 * 7 = 42 then 25 = 4225. To multiply by 11, add neighboring digits: 35 * 11 = 385. Compare fractions by cross-multiplying instead of dividing. Approximate when the options are far apart.
bullets: Use the fraction-percent table you memorized.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Sales were 120 in 2022, 150 in 2023 and 135 in 2024. Growth in 2023 = 30 / 120 = 25%. Change in 2024 = -15 / 150 = -10%. The share of 2024 in the three-year total (405) is 135 / 405 = 33.3%.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: Do these:
bullets: Two full DI sets daily with a timer.
Recite squares to 30 and cubes to 15.
Practice approximation with 20 calculations.

mistakes: Misreading units such as thousands versus lakhs.
Calculating percentage change on the wrong base year.
Doing full long division when the options allow approximation.
takeaways: Read the title, units and labels first.
Most DI questions use percentage change, share, ratio or average.
Shortcuts and approximation save the most time.

title: 30-day English speaking system
summary: Build fluent, clear speaking with a daily TED, record and review loop that you can measure.
why: Placement interviews are won by clear communication as often as by technical skill. Speaking improves with daily recorded practice and honest review, not with passive listening alone.

sections.heading: The 30-minute daily loop
sections.body: Watch one short TED talk (8 minutes). Write 3 new words and 1 useful phrase (4 minutes). Record a 2-minute video summary in your own words (3 minutes). Review it (8 minutes). Re-record an improved version on alternate days (5 minutes).
bullets: Use this structure when you speak: topic, two key points, your opinion.
Keep the videos private.

sections.heading: What to measure
sections.body: Count filler words (um, uh, basically), words per minute (aim for roughly 120 to 150), long pauses, and whether your last sentence sounds finished. Compare Day 1 with Day 30 to see progress.
bullets: Use your phone's voice typing to see which words are misrecognized.
Silence is better than a filler.

sections.heading: Four weekly stages
sections.body: Week 1: speak for 1 minute without stopping. Week 2: 90 seconds with fewer fillers. Week 3: 2 minutes with a clear beginning, middle and end. Week 4: record 'Tell me about yourself' every Sunday and improve it, then explain one solved DSA problem aloud.
bullets: Speaking about code is a separate skill: practice it.

sections.heading: Vocabulary and pronunciation
sections.body: Learn 3 words a day and use each in a sentence you say aloud. Shadow the speaker: play a sentence and repeat it together matching rhythm and stress. Slow down at the ends of sentences.
bullets: Use words you can say confidently; fancy words badly pronounced hurt you.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: This week:
bullets: Record 7 videos and log fillers per video.
Say one project explanation in under 2 minutes.
Explain Two Sum aloud as if teaching a friend.

code:
import re

FILLERS = ["um", "uh", "basically", "you know", "kind of", "sort of", "actually"]


def speaking_report(transcript, seconds):
    text = transcript.lower()
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text)
    filler_count = sum(len(re.findall(rf"\b{re.escape(f)}\b", text)) for f in FILLERS)
    wpm = round(len(words) / (seconds / 60))
    pace = "too fast" if wpm > 170 else "too slow" if wpm < 100 else "good pace"
    return {
        "words": len(words),
        "fillers": filler_count,
        "fillers_per_100_words": round(filler_count / len(words) * 100, 1),
        "wpm": wpm,
        "pace": pace,
    }


sample = "Um, so basically I think coding is, you know, fun. Um, I like it."
report = speaking_report(sample, seconds=6)
assert report["words"] == 14 and report["fillers"] == 4
assert report["wpm"] == 140 and report["pace"] == "good pace"
assert report["fillers_per_100_words"] == 28.6

clean = speaking_report("Today I solved two array problems and learned prefix sums.", seconds=5)
assert clean["fillers"] == 0 and clean["wpm"] == 120 and clean["pace"] == "good pace"
print(report)
mistakes: Listening to talks all day but never recording yourself.
Counting words like 'like' as fillers even when they are normal verbs.
Trying to sound fancy instead of clear.
takeaways: Record, review and re-record daily.
Measure fillers per minute and pace.
Practice explaining code aloud, not only speaking in general.

title: HR interviews: STAR answers and Tell me about yourself
summary: Structure every behavioral answer in four parts and prepare a crisp 90-second introduction.
why: HR and managerial rounds decide many offers. A simple structure keeps your answers short, specific and memorable instead of rambling.

sections.heading: The STAR method
sections.body: Situation: the context in one or two sentences. Task: what you were responsible for. Action: what you personally did, step by step. Result: the outcome, with a number if possible, and what you learned. Spend most of the time on Action and Result.
bullets: Say 'I', not 'we', for your own part.
Keep each answer under two minutes.

sections.heading: Tell me about yourself
sections.body: Use present, past, future in about 90 seconds. Present: who you are now (M.Tech, interests, key skills). Past: one or two achievements or projects that prove those skills. Future: what role you want and why this company. Do not read your resume aloud.
bullets: End with a bridge: 'which is why this role excites me'.

sections.heading: The common questions
sections.body: Strengths (with proof), weakness (real, with a fix in progress), failure (what you changed), conflict (calm, solved), why this company (specific), why should we hire you, 5-year goal, gaps or backlogs (honest and short), salary (research and give a range).
bullets: Prepare 5 stories that can be reused across questions.

sections.heading: When you do not know
sections.body: Say what you know, how you would approach it, and what you would look up. Never invent facts. Interviewers value honest reasoning above a confident wrong answer.
bullets: Buy thinking time: 'Let me think about that for a moment'.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: This week:
bullets: Write 5 STAR stories (project, team, failure, deadline, learning).
Record and refine your 90-second introduction.
Practice with a friend using a scorecard.

mistakes: Describing the situation for a full minute and skipping the result.
Saying 'we' for everything so your own contribution is unclear.
Claiming a perfect strength with no weakness.
takeaways: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Introduction = present, past, future in 90 seconds.
Be honest about what you do not know.

title: Resume bullets and project explanation
summary: Write one-page, ATS-friendly resume bullets with measurable results and explain projects in two minutes.
why: A resume gets about 10 seconds of attention, and recruiters often ask about your first project in the interview. Strong bullets and a rehearsed project story give you control of the conversation.

sections.heading: Resume basics
sections.body: Keep it to one page for a fresher. Order: education, skills, projects, internships, achievements. Use a plain single-column layout and standard section names so applicant tracking systems (ATS) can read it. Use PDF, and give links to GitHub and LinkedIn.
bullets: Skip photos, tables and fancy graphics.
List only skills you can discuss.

sections.heading: The bullet formula
sections.body: Action verb + what you did + how (tools) + measurable result. Example: 'Built a REST API with FastAPI and PostgreSQL that served 500 requests per second, cutting response time by 60% using Redis caching.' Numbers make claims believable.
bullets: Start with verbs like built, designed, optimized, reduced, deployed.
Avoid 'responsible for' and 'worked on'.

sections.heading: Two-minute project story
sections.body: Problem (why it exists), your solution and architecture, tech choices and why, one hard challenge and how you solved it, the result, and what you would improve. Prepare the follow-ups: database schema, scaling, testing, security.
bullets: Be ready to open the code and explain any file.

sections.heading: GitHub and LinkedIn
sections.body: Pin your best 3 repositories with clear READMEs: what it does, screenshots, setup steps, tech stack and lessons learned. Keep commits regular and messages meaningful. Make your LinkedIn headline say what you do.
bullets: A deployed link beats a screenshot.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: This week:
bullets: Rewrite every bullet with the formula.
Record a 2-minute project explanation.
Ask two seniors to review the resume.

code:
STRONG_VERBS = {"built", "designed", "developed", "optimized", "reduced", "deployed",
                "implemented", "automated", "improved", "created", "led", "migrated"}


def score_bullet(text):
    words = text.replace(",", " ").split()
    checks = {
        "starts_with_strong_verb": words[0].lower() in STRONG_VERBS,
        "has_number": any(ch.isdigit() for ch in text),
        "good_length": 8 <= len(words) <= 28,
        "no_weak_phrase": not any(p in text.lower() for p in ("responsible for", "worked on")),
    }
    return sum(checks.values()), [name for name, ok in checks.items() if not ok]


good = "Built a REST API with FastAPI and PostgreSQL, cutting response time by 60% using Redis caching."
weak = "Worked on a website for the college."

assert score_bullet(good) == (4, [])
score, problems = score_bullet(weak)
assert score < 4 and "has_number" in problems and "no_weak_phrase" in problems
print(score_bullet(weak))
mistakes: Listing duties instead of results.
Putting skills on the resume that you cannot discuss.
Using a creative layout that ATS cannot read.
takeaways: Action verb + what + how + number.
One page, plain layout, PDF.
Rehearse the two-minute project story and its follow-ups.

title: Placement timeline and company strategy
summary: Plan the months before placements, split daily time sensibly and understand each company type.
why: Placement success is mostly planning and consistency. Knowing what to finish by when, and what each company type tests, stops you from preparing everything at once and finishing nothing.

sections.heading: Month-by-month plan
sections.body: October: arrays, hashing, two pointers, sliding window, binary search. November: stack, queue, trees, heaps. December: graphs and recursion (exam weeks use Minimum Mode). January: dynamic programming and backtracking, start CS core and a main project. February: greedy, trie, revise the full 150-problem list, resume v1. March: company-wise practice, two timed mocks per week, CS core revision. April: mock interviews, weak patterns, HR answers, applications.
bullets: No new topics in the last month; revise and test.
Exams come first: use Minimum Mode (1 problem + 10 minutes of English).

sections.heading: Daily time split
sections.body: For a 3-hour day, a good split is DSA 55%, aptitude 15%, CS core 10%, English 10% and projects 10%. Adjust by weakness every Sunday review: if aptitude mocks score low, shift 15 minutes there.
bullets: Consistency beats intensity: 3 hours daily beats a 10-hour weekend.

sections.heading: Company types
sections.body: Service companies (mass recruiters) test aptitude, basic coding, communication and CS basics in large online tests. Product companies and startups test DSA depth, problem solving, system design basics and projects. Core software and MNC teams mix both, plus domain knowledge for M.Tech roles.
bullets: Prepare aptitude and communication for all of them.

sections.heading: Rounds and off-campus
sections.body: A typical flow is online assessment, technical rounds, managerial round, then HR. Apply off-campus in parallel: ask for referrals on LinkedIn with a short polite message, keep a tracker of company, role, stage and next step, and follow up after one week.
bullets: Learn the offer's CTC breakup: fixed, variable, bonuses and benefits, before you compare offers.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.body: This week:
bullets: Write your own month-by-month plan with dates.
Start a company tracker sheet.
Ask seniors which companies visit and what the rounds were.

mistakes: Starting every topic at once and finishing none.
Ignoring aptitude and communication because DSA feels more important.
Waiting for campus drives instead of applying off-campus early.
takeaways: Follow a month-by-month plan and protect revision time.
Split daily time by weakness and re-balance weekly.
Prepare aptitude and communication for every company type.
